elements.name: GC Write Barrier
aka: Yuasa barrier / Dijkstra barrier / Steele barrier (variants)
elements.what: A small code sequence the compiler or runtime inserts on every pointer store that records or checks the mutated reference (e.g. by marking a card in a card table or appending to a remembered set), so the collector can find cross-generation or concurrently-mutated pointers without rescanning the whole heap.
elements.problem: Generational and incremental/concurrent collectors must know which old-generation or already-scanned objects now point into the young generation or unscanned space; intercepting mutator writes is the only way to track this without full-heap scans.
elements.named_in: Jones, Hosking & Moss, 'The Garbage Collection Handbook: The Art of Automatic Memory Management' (2011), sect. 11.8 'Write barrier mechanisms' incl. 'Card tables' (verified live via O'Reilly index/ToC this session)

elements.name: Safepoint
elements.what: A designated point in generated or interpreted code at which a thread's state (GC roots, stack maps) is fully described and the thread can be safely blocked; the runtime brings all threads to safepoints (via polls, page-protection tricks, or interpreter checks) before running GC, deoptimization, or other global VM operations.
elements.problem: A runtime cannot scan stacks, move objects, or patch code while mutator threads are at arbitrary instructions; restricting global operations to well-described points bounds metadata cost and makes stop-the-world coordination correct and cheap on the fast path.
elements.named_in: OpenJDK, 'HotSpot Glossary of Terms' (openjdk.org, verified live this session); mechanism analyzed in Agesen, 'GC Points in a Threaded Environment' (Sun Labs TR SMLI TR-98-70, 1998)

elements.name: Deoptimization
aka: on-stack replacement (OSR, the frame-replacement mechanism, folded)
elements.what: The runtime invalidates speculatively optimized compiled code and transfers a running activation back to unoptimized code (interpreter or baseline), reconstructing the equivalent stack frames and local state at a mapped program point; the same frame-replacement machinery run upward (OSR entry) promotes a hot running loop into optimized code.
elements.problem: JIT compilers optimize on assumptions (class hierarchy, type profiles, no debugger) that can be invalidated at runtime, and debuggers need source-level state from optimized frames; the runtime must be able to abandon optimized frames mid-execution without losing correctness.
elements.named_in: Hoelzle, Chambers & Ungar, 'Debugging Optimized Code with Dynamic Deoptimization', PLDI 1992 (verified live via selflanguage.org bibliography this session)

elements.name: Hidden Class
elements.what: The runtime assigns each object a shared internal layout descriptor (map/shape/hidden class) recording its property names and slot offsets, transitioning objects between descriptors as properties are added, so objects created the same way share one layout.
elements.problem: Prototype- and dictionary-based languages have no static classes, so naive objects carry per-instance property tables; shared layout descriptors recover class-like memory density and give inline caches a cheap identity to guard on.
elements.named_in: Chambers, Ungar & Lee, 'An Efficient Implementation of SELF, a Dynamically-Typed Object-Oriented Language Based on Prototypes', OOPSLA 1989 (names 'maps'; verified live this session); 'hidden class' is the V8 documentation term

excluded_notable.name: Threaded code / computed-goto dispatch (Bell, CACM 1973)
excluded_notable.why: Already in the catalog: threaded-code (execution-concurrency) with aka direct threading, indirect threading, computed-goto dispatch. Charter candidate rejected as duplicate.

excluded_notable.name: Inline caching / polymorphic inline cache
excluded_notable.why: Already in the catalog: inline-caching (caching-memoization) covers monomorphic/polymorphic/megamorphic ICs. Checked because hidden-class is adjacent; judged genuinely distinct (IC caches per-site lookup results; hidden class is the layout descriptor the IC guards on), so hidden-class added as its own element.

excluded_notable.name: Pointer tagging / NaN-boxing / small-integer tagging
excluded_notable.why: Already in the catalog: pointer-tagging (data-representation) with NaN-boxing and Smi as aka. No new element needed.

excluded_notable.name: Hot code reload
excluded_notable.why: Already in the catalog: hot-code-reload (code-structure). Charter check confirmed present.

excluded_notable.name: On-stack replacement (OSR) as a separate element
excluded_notable.why: Judged per charter: OSR and deoptimization share one frame-replacement mechanism (reconstructing equivalent activation frames at a mapped point, run in either tier direction); at strictness peak folded into deoptimization as aka rather than split into two entries.

excluded_notable.name: Card table / card marking as a separate element
excluded_notable.why: Folded into gc-write-barrier as the dominant implementation variant per one-element-per-mechanism (GC Handbook treats card tables as a write-barrier implementation, sect. 11.8).

excluded_notable.name: Remembered set as a separate element
excluded_notable.why: The data structure a write barrier maintains; GC Handbook ch. 11 treats barrier and remembered set as one recording mechanism. Folded into gc-write-barrier aka as a role.

excluded_notable.name: GC read barrier / load barrier (Brooks pointer, ZGC colored-pointer load barrier)
excluded_notable.why: Established (GC Handbook sect. 11.8 sibling of write barriers) and genuinely absent, but outside this round's charter candidate list and a dual mechanism of narrower reach; at strictness peak recorded here rather than added. Flag for the editor if VM coverage is later deepened.

excluded_notable.name: Tri-color marking / mark-sweep / copying collection
excluded_notable.why: Covered by the existing garbage-collection element's aka set (mark-sweep, mark-compact, copying collection); no separate entry warranted.

excluded_notable.name: Interpreter dispatch loop (switch dispatch)
excluded_notable.why: Covered between bytecode-virtual-machine (bytecode interpreter) and threaded-code (dispatch variants); a separate 'dispatch loop' entry would duplicate both.

notes: Final-round strictness applied. Charter listed 5 candidate mechanisms; 1 (threaded code) was already present verbatim, 4 were genuinely absent and all are canonical VM-implementation literature: GC write barrier (Jones/Hosking/Moss 2011, live-verified sect. 11.8), safepoint (OpenJDK HotSpot Glossary live-verified; Agesen TR-98-70), deoptimization (Hoelzle/Chambers/Ungar PLDI 1992, live-verified), hidden class (Chambers/Ungar/Lee OOPSLA 1989 'maps', live-verified; canonical name taken from the dominant modern cross-engine term). Judgment calls: OSR folded into deoptimization (one frame-replacement mechanism); card table and remembered set folded into gc-write-barrier; hidden-class kept separate from inline-caching (layout descriptor vs per-site lookup cache). Safepoint filed under synchronization-coordination (its essence is bringing all threads to a coordinated blockable state), deoptimization under execution-concurrency alongside the other runtime-execution machinery. No architecture-level parks. Yield: 4 new, 0 borderline — consistent with a nearly saturated vein whose remaining gaps were exactly the charter's pre-identified candidates.
